title: The Gang Gets New Wheels

jokes.text: Dennis gathers the Gang and delivers a solemn preamble implying a major personal revelation, building anticipation for a weighty emotional confession
jokes.setup: Dennis speaks with grave seriousness about his absence, says the Gang has 'burning questions' and he's ready to 'open it up'
jokes.punchline: The only thing he cares about is where his car is
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis narcissism misdirection: he builds a fake emotional moment about his family/absence, then pivots immediately to his Range Rover. The structure is excellent — the longer he talks about privacy and respect, the harder the punchline lands. Deeply character-specific; only Dennis would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dennis dramatically announces he's ready for questions about his absence, but no one has been wondering about his personal life

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie's total indifference to Dennis's big emotional moment — 'I don't care. Do you care?' / 'I mean, it doesn't really...'
jokes.setup: Dennis expects the Gang to be burning with curiosity about his life
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie are completely, genuinely unbothered and cannot even muster fake concern
jokes.explanation: The Gang's total apathy is pitch-perfect character comedy. The economy is great — they don't even bother finishing sentences. It amplifies Dennis's delusion by contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't care. Do you care?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I mean, it doesn't really...

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Sometimes it's best to raise a family from a distance. And that's what I've decided to do, okay? And I'm not the first man in history to ever do it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is apparently trying to explain his absence from his family
jokes.punchline: He delivers a horrifying parenting philosophy with total conviction and no self-awareness, asserting historical precedent for abandonment
jokes.explanation: Perfectly encapsulates Dennis's self-justifying sociopathy. The 'I'm not the first man in history' is a brilliantly lazy rationalization that tells us everything about his character. Quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Sometimes it's best to raise a family from a distance. And that's what I've decided to do, okay? And I'm not the first man in history to ever do it.

jokes.text: Cut to the Range Rover destroyed/vandalized while left on the street — Dennis says 'Goddamn it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis confidently states his car is 'right where you left it' as if that's reassuring
jokes.punchline: The car has clearly been destroyed/stripped; Dennis's groan is the punctuation
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff is efficient and well-structured. It's a standard 'thing is worse than expected' beat, elevated by Dennis's simple 'Goddamn it' — maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I mean, you guys wouldn't really understand 'cause you've never owned a vehicle.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We own vehicles.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah? Name one.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, we had those matching Mongoose bikes back in the day.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie reminisce about their matching Mongoose bikes and suggest bikes as transportation — the car dealership doesn't have bikes
jokes.setup: Dennis mourns his Range Rover as part of his identity
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's solution is Mongoose bikes, treating them as equivalent replacements for a luxury SUV
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific absurdism. Mac and Charlie's earnest pivot to bikes in a car dealership perfectly captures their child-brain energy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's the Kelley Blue Book value of your car

jokes.text: Dennis at the dealership: the car 'sort of lacks the original's masculinity and beefiness, you know, but there's a grace to it that I-I think I could probably work with'
jokes.setup: Dennis is looking at a new car
jokes.punchline: He evaluates the car as if appraising a romantic partner, using gendered physical descriptors — revealing his psychology
jokes.explanation: Nicely character-specific. Dennis's objectifying language applied to a car is a small but telling joke about how he processes everything through dominance and appearance.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You never bought me a Range Rover. All I got were shit cars, which you guys crashed, and you certainly never reimbursed me.

jokes.text: Dennis tries to pass Frank off to the salesperson for financing, and Dee protests: 'You never bought me a Range Rover. All I got were shit cars, which you guys crashed.'
jokes.setup: Dennis confidently delegates financing to Frank
jokes.punchline: Dee calls out the asymmetry — the Gang has always gotten Dee the worst deal possible — delivered with her signature exasperated fury
jokes.explanation: Functional Dee-abuse joke with solid character logic. The Gang routinely exploits Dee, and her outrage is a reliable source of modest laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Car Salesman
dialogue.line: Your driver's license is expired.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Since when?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Quit your squawking, Dee' and immediately redirects to Frank for the money
jokes.setup: Dee has a legitimate grievance
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses her entirely with a bird insult ('squawking') and moves on without a beat
jokes.explanation: 'Squawking' is a good word choice — consistent with the show's bird-related Dee insults — and the dismissal is totally economical.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dork.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Jump this manhole.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Nice.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, still got the skid.

jokes.text: Frank hands Dennis $473 as the Kelley Blue Book value of his destroyed Range Rover
jokes.setup: Dennis expects compensation for his car; Frank acts as though he's being generous
jokes.punchline: The payout is $473 — a comically insufficient amount delivered with total Frank sincerity
jokes.explanation: The specific dollar amount ($473) makes this land — it's precise enough to feel researched and petty. Frank's total confidence in the offer is great character work.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So Shawn Dumont didn't just steal our bikes. He stole our identity.

jokes.text: The salesperson tells Frank his driver's license is expired — since 1984
jokes.setup: Frank confidently hands over his driver's license to buy a new car
jokes.punchline: His license has been expired since 1984 — implying he has been driving illegally for nearly 40 years
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specific year (1984) is doing enormous work — it's a perfect Frank Reynolds detail implying decades of criminal driving and total disregard for society. The beat after ('Whoo! Yeah, man!') suggests the Gang celebrates this. Highly quotable and character-defining.

dialogue.speaker: Kids
dialogue.line: You guys look like you're 40.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, we are 40.

dialogue.speaker: Kids
dialogue.line: Gay!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, well, I am gay, but he's not my boyfriend, 'cause I could do much better than him.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie on bikes: 'Dork. Jump this manhole.' followed by bike tricks with the energy of 12-year-olds
jokes.setup: Two grown men in their 40s are riding bikes
jokes.punchline: They immediately regress to pure childlike id — doing manhole jumps, saying 'radical,' calling each other dork
jokes.explanation: The regression is very on-brand for Mac and Charlie. 'Radical' is a great period-specific word choice for their arrested development. Modest but reliable laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, well, well, I am gay, but he's not my boyfriend, 'cause I could do much better than him.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I feel like a carefree, young kid on a bike again, man. World at my fingertips.' — leads to the revelation that Shawn Dumont stole their bikes and therefore their identity
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie wax nostalgic about bikes
jokes.punchline: The philosophical leap that stolen bikes = stolen identity is treated with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the episode's B-plot engine. The identity theme is introduced here with appropriate absurdist sincerity. Echoes the Dennis/Range Rover theme cleverly.

jokes.text: "It's like what you ride is your identity... so Shawn Dumont didn't just steal our bikes. He stole our identity."
jokes.setup: Mac connects Dennis's speech about the Range Rover being part of his identity to their bikes
jokes.punchline: He concludes with complete sincerity that a childhood bully stole their entire adult identities
jokes.explanation: Mac applying Dennis's narcissistic philosophy earnestly to their situation is good character work, and the leap from 'bikes' to 'entire identities' is a solid absurdist escalation. Functions as thematic connective tissue for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What up, ding-dong?

jokes.text: 'What are you gonna do about it?' — Shawn Dumont's line, quoted as 'the perfect line' that 'ends all conversations'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie recall the moment Shawn Dumont dared them to reclaim their stolen bikes
jokes.punchline: They both agree it's philosophically unanswerable — 'You just got to walk away, 'cause it's the end of the conversation'
jokes.explanation: Smart setup for a running gag. The joke is that Mac and Charlie have deep respect for the rhetorical power of a bully's taunt, treating it like a philosophical koan. This pays off beautifully at the end. High quotability and strong episode architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I tell you what, I am loving it. And Brenda, you got to upgrade, you stupid bitch. Okay? Don't be a dumb idiot.

jokes.text: A cool kid rolls up on a bike and says 'Cool bikes.' — Mac and Charlie are thrilled, then the kid immediately: 'You guys look like you're 40.'
jokes.setup: Kid appears to be complimenting Mac and Charlie's bikes
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts them by noting they look 40 (they are 40) — the bikes can't fix that
jokes.explanation: The brief compliment followed by the age insult is well-timed. 'Well, we are 40' is the ideal straight-man response — accepting and devastated simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: There's nothing in this book about the Asians. You can't be PC on the road and expect to live.

jokes.text: Kid: 'Do you have the same bike as your boyfriend? Gay!' — Mac: 'Oh, well, I am gay, but he's not my boyfriend, 'cause I could do much better than him.'
jokes.setup: Kid uses 'gay' as a schoolyard insult
jokes.punchline: Mac accepts the first premise but rejects the second, turning it into a sincere statement about his romantic standards
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. Mac's response is perfectly constructed — he doesn't take offense at 'gay' but is deeply wounded by the implication that Charlie is his boyfriend. The 'I could do much better' is both hilarious and a great character note. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Teen
dialogue.line: Bruh, that shit was hilarious. You're gonna fail so hard, man.

jokes.text: Mac: 'It's difficult out there. You guys will understand when you get older.'
jokes.setup: Mac is talking to literal children about his dating difficulties
jokes.punchline: He delivers a world-weary adult wisdom line to kids about the gay dating scene, completely inverting the expected dynamic
jokes.explanation: Mac's sincerity here is key — he's not being ironic, he genuinely is offering life advice to children. The gap between his perspective and reality is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: John
dialogue.line: Am I your Uber?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, I...

dialogue.speaker: John
dialogue.line: Oh, okay.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, I think I see what's happening here.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Don't push your agenda on them.' Mac: 'I'm not pushing an agenda. I'm just saying statistically at least one of them...' Kids: 'You guys suck.'
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining his dating difficulties to children
jokes.punchline: The kids cut it off with a flat 'You guys suck' before Mac can finish his statistical argument
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation joke. The kids' dismissal is funnier than whatever Mac was going to say. The unfinished statistical argument is a nice piece of character absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's a strong economy name. You know, it says so much, yet it says so little.

jokes.text: Dennis pulls up in a small economy car (Prius) and tries to present it as cool — 'She's quiet. But that's a virtue. Stealth.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is a Range Rover man who lost his car
jokes.punchline: He's now desperately spinning a Prius as equivalent — using the word 'stealth' for a hybrid's quiet engine
jokes.explanation: Dennis's rationalization engine running at full speed. 'Stealth' is a great word choice — it's the most macho possible spin on 'silent hybrid.' Strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's a strong economy name. You know, it says so much, yet it says so little. ... Yeah, you got a good economy face on you, too.

jokes.text: Dennis spots the valet and says 'Probably doesn't speak English' — but the valet does and is visibly there
jokes.setup: Dennis pulls up to a fancy hotel/restaurant valet in his Prius
jokes.punchline: He mutters a racist assumption about the valet right in front of him, exposing his oblivious bigotry
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy showing Dennis's casual racism. The show uses this as character exposure rather than endorsement. The payoff when the valet speaks English is decent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa. I got a Chuck Knoblauch!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's, like, pre-yips, man.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Pre-yips?

jokes.text: Dee pulls up in Frank's Range Rover while Dennis is in a Prius — role reversal
jokes.setup: Dennis lost his Range Rover; Dee has never had a nice car
jokes.punchline: Dee is now driving the Range Rover and loving it while Dennis is in the economy car she'd normally get
jokes.explanation: Good structural irony. The visual of Dee looking down at Dennis from the Range Rover is a perfect inversion. Well-integrated into the episode's identity theme.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa. I got a Chuck Knoblauch! That's, like, pre-yips, man.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Pre-yips?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That could be worth a fortune!

jokes.text: Dee explains to Dennis that she's driving it because Frank is at driver's ed — 'I showed him how to drive stick last night' (said later, but the driver's ed detail lands here)
jokes.setup: Frank's license has been expired since 1984
jokes.punchline: Frank is genuinely in driver's ed like a teenager — the logical consequence of the license joke
jokes.explanation: Solid callback payoff. The image of Frank in driver's ed is funny and consistent. It earns its laugh by following through on the license joke's logic.

jokes.text: Dee explains the Range Rover dynamic: 'It's kind of like you're up on a throne, and you're looking down on all the minions'
jokes.setup: Dee is suddenly driving the Range Rover Dennis wanted
jokes.punchline: She has immediately absorbed Dennis's exact power fantasy and is delivering his own philosophy back at him from his throne
jokes.explanation: Good character mirror. Dee has become Dennis-lite in his absence, which is both funny and slightly sad. The 'throne/minions' language is perfectly Range Rover-bro.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, Karen, you bitch. You dumb idiot. You stupid savage.

jokes.text: Rich woman asks if Dennis is 'loving' his car — he enthusiastically agrees, then pivots: 'And Brenda, you got to upgrade, you stupid bitch. Okay? Don't be a dumb idiot.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is sucking up to wealthy women at a valet line; Karen asks if he's loving his Range Rover
jokes.punchline: He enthusiastically trash-talks Brenda to ingratiate himself with Karen, using cartoonishly harsh language ('stupid bitch,' 'dumb idiot') as if this is normal social behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Dennis's social maneuvering is so aggressive and tone-deaf — roasting Brenda directly to her face with slurs while trying to charm Karen. The specific phrase 'dumb idiot' stacked on 'stupid bitch' shows his vocabulary disintegrates when excited. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dennis's awkward attempts to hit on Tara, mentioning farts and twins

jokes.text: Karen: 'Oh, you are fun.' — then immediately turns cold when she discovers Dennis drove a Prius: 'So you don't have a Range Rover... Then why are we talking to you?'
jokes.setup: Karen seems charmed by Dennis's aggressive behavior
jokes.punchline: The moment she hears 'Prius' she drops him completely — the car is literally the only thing that matters to these women
jokes.explanation: Sharp and efficient. 'Then why are we talking to you?' is excellent — it's the same rhetorical kill-shot energy as 'What are you gonna do about it?' The shallowness is so pure it's funny. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Teen
dialogue.line: You lose your mojo?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I didn't lose my mojo.

dialogue.speaker: Teen
dialogue.line: Yeah, you got it.

dialogue.speaker: Teen
dialogue.line: You got the moves?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I got my mojo.

jokes.text: Frank in driver's ed: 'What you want to do is, you want to lurch into the intersection. It's like a game of chicken.'
jokes.setup: Driver's ed instructor asks who has right of way at a four-way stop
jokes.punchline: Frank gives confident, specific, completely wrong advice based on his actual driving philosophy
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank Reynolds energy. 'You lurch, and then you lurch, you lurch some more' — the repetition of 'lurch' is somehow very funny. Frank teaching driver's ed students the wrong rules with total confidence is excellent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dude, I'll suck you.
You'll suck me?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, that's... That's not what I meant.

jokes.text: Frank: 'There's nothing in this book about the Asians. You can't be PC on the road and expect to live.'
jokes.setup: Frank dismisses the driver's ed manual as not covering 'real' road rules
jokes.punchline: His specific racist driving theory delivered with life-or-death seriousness to a class of teenagers
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank — the racism is meant to expose him as a terrible person, not validate the belief. The 'you will die' stakes elevation is funny. Docked slightly on earned_vs_cheap because the ethnic stereotype is a lazy comedic shortcut even within the show's framework.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What are you, what are you gonna do with that, dude?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Go hit on the girl, will you?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'll show you what sucks, huh?

jokes.text: Driver's ed instructor: 'We are out of time for today. I urge you all to study what's in the book and not listen to this man.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just destroyed the class with wrong and racist driving advice
jokes.punchline: The instructor's tired, formal dismissal of Frank — 'not listen to this man' — is hilariously understated for the chaos Frank caused
jokes.explanation: The straight-man punctuation on Frank's chaos. 'Not listen to this man' as a formal instruction to students is a great deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, no. It makes me... makes me fart. I don't want to, I don't want to fart right now.

jokes.text: High schooler: 'Bruh, that shit was hilarious. You're gonna fail so hard, man.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just humiliated himself in driver's ed
jokes.punchline: A teenager's casual Gen-Z verdict on Frank's performance — treating a grown man like a peer who bombed a test
jokes.explanation: Decent but functional. The kid treating Frank as a peer is good, though the slang dates the joke slightly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, she farts a shit ton, man. / Yeah. I-I don't have that. Like, everything makes her... everything makes her fart.

jokes.text: Frank tries to bribe a teenager to let him cheat off his test — offers beer, cigs, weed, blow, porno
jokes.setup: Frank needs to pass driver's ed and asks to cheat off a teenager
jokes.punchline: The kid rejects each bribe because he already has access to all of them — he's in high school
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating joke. The structure is perfect — Frank offers increasingly illicit bribes, and each one is casually rebuffed because teenagers have everything. 'Nah, I never get carded' / 'Dude, I've got a phone' / 'I'm in high school, man, I can get all that shit.' Frank's bribery menu is perfectly Frank. The 'real thing' (porn magazines presumably / adult contact) as the final offer that works is dark and very funny.

jokes.text: A stranger (John) gets into Dennis's Prius thinking it's his Uber
jokes.setup: Dennis is sitting in a Prius
jokes.punchline: The car is so bland and anonymous that a stranger mistakes it for an Uber — the ultimate insult to Dennis's identity
jokes.explanation: Smart conceptual joke. The Prius-as-Uber is the logical extension of the economy car theme — Dennis has become invisible. Reinforces the identity thesis while being genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I am a golden goddess, you idiot. Savage idiots! And I banged your man.

jokes.text: John: 'Nothing to be ashamed of. It's very sensible.' — Dennis's visible struggle to accept this
jokes.setup: John means to be reassuring about the Prius
jokes.punchline: His reassurance is the insult — 'sensible' is the last thing Dennis wants to be
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe. Dennis being consoled for having a sensible car is torture for his character — the gap between his self-image and reality is the whole joke.

dialogue.line: The revelation that Aidan is Karen's teenage son, not her boy toy husband

jokes.text: "That's a strong economy name. It says so much, yet it says so little." / "You got a good economy face on you, too."
jokes.setup: Dennis meets John and starts adopting 'economy' as a framework for evaluating everything
jokes.punchline: He invents the concept of 'economy names' and 'economy faces' — evaluating John's features through the lens of his new Prius life
jokes.explanation: Very funny Dennis bit. His attempt to find a philosophical framework for the Prius — 'economy names,' 'economy faces' — reveals how hard his brain is working to maintain superiority even in defeat. 'It says so much, yet it says so little' as a compliment is perfectly absurd. Dennis inventing an entire aesthetic category on the fly to cope is very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Karen
dialogue.line: Oh, my God. You're the creepy old man from Aidan's Instagram stories.

jokes.text: Dennis spiraling into 'economy logic': 'This economy car has got me thinking I could enjoy economy activities'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been talking to John about fantasy sports
jokes.punchline: Dennis concludes that his car has fundamentally altered his identity and aesthetic preferences — 'economy activities'
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier Dennis moments. The episode's thesis — that your vehicle IS your identity — is taken to its logical extreme. Dennis is not examining a new car; he is becoming a new person. 'Economy activities' is a great coinage.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Jonathan!

dialogue.speaker: John
dialogue.line: What's up?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What is this? What am I seeing?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You know what, John. Cancel your ride. I'll drive you to your fantasy.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just convinced himself he is now an 'economy man'
jokes.punchline: He delivers this line with the full seductive confidence of his Range Rover persona, but applied to giving a stranger a ride to fantasy baseball
jokes.explanation: 'I'll drive you to your fantasy' is unintentionally creepy in a Dennis-specific way. His seductive register applied to mundane logistics is a consistently funny character note.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Be gone from me now.
What?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Be gone from me, you soy boy beta cuck.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie buying baseball cards and Mac holds up a Chuck Knoblauch: 'That's like pre-yips, man. That could be worth a fortune!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are buying baseball cards on their bikes, acting like children
jokes.punchline: Mac's excited investment logic about Knoblauch's pre-yips value — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Good for baseball fans — 'pre-yips Knoblauch' is a genuinely funny specific detail. The idea that this card is a hot investment while they're riding bikes is delightfully childlike.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We did a bad thing, dude. I think I killed a kid.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He did. I saw him. I think the kid's dead.

jokes.text: Charlie's bike is gone — 'Ah, shit.' — immediately stolen while they were talking
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are celebrating their bikes and nostalgia
jokes.punchline: Charlie's bike is immediately stolen — the cycle (pun intended) repeats
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy of storytelling. The callback to stolen bikes happens immediately after the nostalgic discussion, with zero fanfare. 'Ah, shit' is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I almost got T-boned by an Asian driver and it was totally my fault. She did everything by the book. Very surprising.

jokes.text: Frank's porn stash reveal — stored in plastic bags labeled 'Trésor' and 'Skank'
jokes.setup: Frank promised the high schooler 'the real thing' in terms of pornography
jokes.punchline: Frank's porn collection is in labeled plastic bags with names like 'Trésor' and 'Skank' — a bizarrely organized physical archive
jokes.explanation: One of the best Frank jokes in the episode. The labeling system is so specifically deranged — 'Trésor' (French for treasure) next to 'Skank' suggests an organized pervert's curation system. The high schooler's reaction ('This shit's just weird as hell') is the perfect straight-man response. High originality.

jokes.text: High schooler wants to put the magazine on his Instagram story — holds it up for a photo
jokes.setup: Frank is showing off his physical porn collection
jokes.punchline: The teenager's reflex is to Instagram it — the magazine is so retro it's become content to him, not pornography
jokes.explanation: Smart generational joke. For the teen, the magazine is a novelty artifact — Instagram content — not titillation. The irony is sharp.

jokes.text: Dee in the Range Rover, talking to herself about being invited to Turks and Caicos on a private jet: 'That's when I was like, okay, well, which one is it? Turks or Caicos? 'Cause I'm not invited back on Caicos.'
jokes.setup: Dee is describing how the Range Rover women accepted her and invited her on a trip
jokes.punchline: She's apparently been banned from Caicos specifically — a throwaway detail implying a prior incident never explained
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Dee casually mentions she's not 'invited back on Caicos' with zero explanation — the specificity is perfect. We don't need to know what happened; the fact that she's been banned from one half of a hyphenated island destination tells us everything. Genuinely quotable and original. The valet's silent reaction ('Why aren't you laughing?') is the button.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Why aren't you laughing?' Valet: 'I speak English. It's just not funny.'
jokes.setup: Dee has been treating the valet as a non-English speaker all episode; she tells a story and expects a laugh
jokes.punchline: The valet speaks perfect English and his critique is exactly right — 'It's just not funny'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff and one of the episode's best lines. The valet's flat 'It's just not funny' is devastating — it simultaneously calls out Dee's racism (she assumed he couldn't understand) and genuinely critiques her storytelling. Perfect economy. The double meaning (he heard everything they said all episode) makes this a rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Karen: 'I just wish my second husband came with a dimmer switch. I forgot how much energy men in their 20s have.'
jokes.setup: Rich women are bonding at a spa
jokes.punchline: Karen's complaint about her young trophy husband's energy — 'dimmer switch' — is an elegantly horrible metaphor treating a person like an appliance
jokes.explanation: 'Dimmer switch' is a great image. It's the perfect complaint of a wealthy older woman with a boy toy — she wants less of him, not none. Sharp economy and quotable.

jokes.text: Karen: 'You don't have to worry about these things 'cause you've never been married.' — Dee's internal reaction is a seething pause
jokes.setup: Karen seems to be accepting Dee as an equal
jokes.punchline: Karen casually weaponizes Dee's marital status — the slight is so smooth and social it barely registers as an attack until it lands
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup. Karen's socially coded insult is exactly how wealthy women stab each other — through seeming compliments. Dee's internal processing of this is where the comedy lives.

jokes.text: Dee's internal monologue: 'Oh, Karen, you bitch. You dumb idiot. You stupid savage. You're not the alpha here, you crusty-ass fool. Oh, I'm gonna cuck you so hard. Your boy toy... he's mine. I will destroy you. I am a 2018 Range Rover woman. I am a golden goddess.'
jokes.setup: Karen has insulted Dee's marital status
jokes.punchline: Dee's internal spiral devolves from a standard revenge fantasy into Range Rover identity affirmations and sexual warfare declarations
jokes.explanation: Excellent extended character moment. Dee's insult vocabulary ('crusty-ass fool,' 'stupid savage') escalates hilariously, and the pivot to 'I am a 2018 Range Rover woman / I am a golden goddess' is perfect — she has fully absorbed the car-as-identity thesis and weaponized it. 'Cuck you so hard' is unexpected and very funny. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dee's internal monologue: "Oh, Karen, you bitch. You dumb idiot. You stupid savage." / "You're not the alpha here, you crusty-ass fool." / "Oh, I'm gonna cuck you so hard."
jokes.setup: Karen has insulted Dee's marital status
jokes.punchline: Dee's internal response escalates from generic insults to a declaration of sexual warfare — she'll seduce Karen's husband to assert dominance
jokes.explanation: 'I am gonna cuck you so hard' as Dee's battle plan is both absurd and completely in character. The escalation from 'bitch' through 'crusty-ass fool' to sexual revenge strategy is very funny. 'I am a 2018 Range Rover woman. I am a golden goddess.' is a great character delusion line. Dee's inner monologue reveals how Range Rover identity has become a war machine for her.

jokes.text: Frank and the high schooler (Aidan) crash Dennis's fantasy baseball gathering — Dennis introduces Frank as 'my friend Frank and his... young friend. His... uh...'
jokes.setup: Dennis has ingratiated himself with normal guys at their house
jokes.punchline: He cannot introduce Frank and Aidan without stumbling — the optics of a 70-year-old man with a teenage boy are clearly alarming to him
jokes.explanation: Dennis's failing composure as he introduces the creepy pairing is good cringe. His trailing off on 'his, uh... young friend' shows his social intelligence recognizing the problem without having a solution.

jokes.text: Aidan: 'This place is weak, bro.' — Dennis's immediate panic and over-explanation to the room
jokes.setup: Dennis has finally found a cool social group and is trying hard to fit in
jokes.punchline: The teenager he brought immediately insults the host's apartment, blowing Dennis's cover
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe. Dennis's social investment undone by the teenager he's bribed. Standard but well-executed.

jokes.text: Frank goads Dennis into hitting on Tara: 'You lose your mojo?' — Dennis insists he has his mojo, then Frank does an Insta story
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he still has his old confidence
jokes.punchline: Dennis cannot even figure out how to do an Instagram story and flails pathetically in front of a teenager
jokes.explanation: Good character deflation. The mojo claim is immediately tested and immediately fails. The Instagram fumble reinforces the mid-life identity crisis theme.

jokes.text: Dennis's attempt to flirt with Tara: starts with hat twins, mentions his twin sister, says she 'farts a shit ton,' and pivots to the Minnesota Twins
jokes.setup: Dennis is supposed to demonstrate his legendary mojo
jokes.punchline: His flirting is a catastrophic word salad from hats to farting twins to baseball — a complete mojo collapse
jokes.explanation: The best extended comedic sequence in the episode. Dennis — who has spent seasons terrorizing women with calculated manipulation — has completely lost his fastball. The escalation is perfect: 'hat twins' (mildly weird) → 'I am a twin' (oversharing) → 'my sister farts a shit ton' (inexplicable derailment) → 'The Minnesota Twins, you know what I'm saying?' (panicked pivot). Each beat is worse than the last. This is exceptional character comedy because it requires knowing Dennis's history to fully appreciate the collapse. 'She farts a shit ton' is the highest peak of absurdism.

jokes.text: "Oh, this dude sucks." / "What are you doing, man? I don't suck. Dude, I'll suck you." / "You'll suck me?"
jokes.setup: Teen says Dennis sucks at Instagram
jokes.punchline: Dennis's flustered response — 'I'll suck you' — creates an accidental sexual offer; both parties immediately register the unintended meaning
jokes.explanation: Accidental double entendre executed with good timing. Dennis's horror at what he just said is a good reaction beat. The rhythm — insult, flustered comeback, immediate recognition of the problem — is tight.

jokes.text: "I noticed you were wearing a hat, and that's pretty cool. Like, I don't see a lot of girls wearing hats, you know, and I'm wearing a hat, too, you know. It's like we're... It's like we're hat twins."
jokes.setup: Dennis pivots from the farting disaster and tries another approach
jokes.punchline: 'Hat twins' — Dennis's most pathetic pickup attempt, completely devoid of his usual manipulative charm
jokes.explanation: One of the funniest moments in the episode and potentially the season. Dennis Reynolds delivering 'hat twins' as a flirt line is a catastrophic reversal of his entire character. This is a man who has bragged about his elaborate seduction methods across 13 seasons. The halting construction — 'It's like we're... It's like we're hat twins' — suggests even Dennis doesn't believe what he's saying. It's deeply earned by everything the episode has built. The Prius has genuinely broken him. Approaches the CRAFT 9.5 anchor benchmark for character integration and earned comedy.

jokes.text: Tara: 'I'm gonna get back in there.' Dennis: 'Yeah. The Minnesota Twins. You know what I'm saying?' Tara: '...Yeah, they're a team.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just said something completely non-sequitur about the Minnesota Twins
jokes.punchline: Tara's flat, charitable answer — 'Yeah, they're a team' — and her immediate exit is perfect straight-man delivery
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the flirting sequence. 'Yeah, they're a team' is exactly what someone says when they're being kind but escaping a disaster. The economy is impeccable — four words carry enormous comedic weight as the punctuation on a 90-second trainwreck.

jokes.text: "Yeah, I-I don't have that." — Dennis clarifying he doesn't fart as much as his sister
jokes.setup: Dennis has just revealed his sister farts constantly; Tara is clearly not interested
jokes.punchline: Dennis's clarification — that he personally doesn't fart as much — implies he thinks this detail is what might save the conversation
jokes.explanation: The understated delivery of 'Yeah, I-I don't have that' as Dennis's most desperate attempt to rehabilitate the conversation is beautiful. It acknowledges that he knows this has been a disaster. The implication that 'I fart less than my sister' might salvage a seduction is tragically deluded.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie track down the kid who stole Charlie's bike — but the dad is Shawn Dumont, their childhood bully
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie confront the kid who stole their bike
jokes.punchline: The father who appears to mediate is Shawn Dumont — the original bike thief from 30 years ago
jokes.explanation: Structurally satisfying callback. The fact that Mac and Charlie's childhood nemesis has a son who is now also stealing bikes from them is a perfect generational joke about their perpetual victimhood.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That's Shawn Dumont. He got fat as shit, man. I almost didn't recognize him.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie realize the father is their old bully
jokes.punchline: Mac's first observation about their nemesis is that he got fat — no anger, just an aesthetic assessment
jokes.explanation: Decent observation. The fact that Mac's big reaction to his childhood nemesis is about weight is both petty and very Mac. Not exceptional but consistently funny.

jokes.text: Shawn Dumont (the dad) says 'What are you gonna do about it?' — Mac and Charlie say nothing, turn, and walk away defeated
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie built up to confronting Shawn Dumont for 30 years of stolen identity
jokes.punchline: He uses the exact same line; they still have no answer and walk away with nothing
jokes.explanation: The best payoff in the episode and one of the stronger structural jokes of the season. The setup was laid out perfectly — they established the line's philosophical power, spent the episode preparing for revenge, and when the moment comes, the exact same line from the grown-up bully produces the exact same result. Mac and Charlie's silent walk of shame is comedy gold. The generational rhyme (his son now steals their bikes too) makes it even richer. This earns its near-perfect scores.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie walking away: 'Dude, it's the perfect line, dude. There's no coming back from that.' 'Son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: They've just been defeated by the same line again
jokes.punchline: Their response is to once again intellectually validate the line that just defeated them — not anger, but academic appreciation
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the running gag. Mac and Charlie's inability to feel pure anger — instead they're genuinely impressed by the line that just owned them — is precisely the kind of delusional character-consistent comedy the show does best. 'Son of a bitch' as the final word is the ideal emotional punctuation.

jokes.text: Dee confronts Karen at the door: 'I've seen them real up close and personal' about the bed linens — implying she slept with Aidan
jokes.setup: Karen mentions her Egyptian cotton 1,000 thread count linens
jokes.punchline: Dee drops the revelation that she slept with Aidan (Karen's boy toy/son, it will turn out) using this as the vehicle
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the episode's big cringe payoff. Dee's 'You heard me' energy is excellent. The linens as the vehicle for the reveal is a smart piece of writing.

jokes.text: "I was just telling Brenda about my new bed linens. Egyptian cotton. 1,000 thread count. You got to see them." / "Oh, I-I've seen them. I've seen them real up close and personal."
jokes.setup: Dee approaches Karen's door
jokes.punchline: The sheets callback lands — Dee has slept in Karen's bed with Karen's husband
jokes.explanation: The sheets callback pays off Dee's revenge plot efficiently. The reprise of the Egyptian cotton dialogue with Dee's loaded response is well-constructed — it makes Karen repeat the setup unwittingly. Dark, well-earned.

jokes.text: Dee in full goddess mode: 'I am a golden goddess, you idiot. Savage idiots! And I banged your man.'
jokes.setup: Dee has followed through on her cuck-Karen plan
jokes.punchline: She delivers the reveal with the exact same Range Rover goddess language from her internal monologue, now externalized and even more absurd
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to her internal monologue — she actually followed through, and the language matches exactly. 'And I banged your man' as the climax of the goddess speech is hilariously crude after all the grandiosity.

jokes.text: "This spinster spun a web that swallowed your boy toy up whole. I am a goddess."
jokes.setup: Dee has successfully slept with Karen's husband
jokes.punchline: She announces her victory in the most overwrought possible terms — 'spinster spun a web' — while Karen is bewildered
jokes.explanation: The 'spinster spun a web' line is funny for its self-aware use of the word 'spinster' (the insult she was stung by) now repurposed as a weapon. Dee reclaiming 'spinster' as predator imagery is sharp. 'I am a goddess' callback to her earlier inner monologue is satisfying.

jokes.text: It's revealed Aidan is Karen's SON, not her husband — 'Aidan's my son!'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee both believe Aidan is Karen's boy-toy husband
jokes.punchline: Aidan is her teenage son — meaning both Frank (who showed him porn and bribed him) and Dee (who slept with him) have done something much worse
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's biggest structural payoffs. The reveal recontextualizes everything: Frank's driver's ed subplot (Aidan was his classmate/bribe recipient), the Instagram porn story, and Dee's 'cucking Karen' plan. The economy is exceptional — one line detonates three plotlines simultaneously. High impact and strong craft.

jokes.text: Frank: 'What's that?' — not registering the horror of the revelation at all
jokes.setup: Karen has revealed Aidan is her son, not her husband
jokes.punchline: Frank's completely blank, uncomprehending response — 'What's that?' — suggests the information hasn't landed as a problem for him
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word joke. Frank's 'What's that?' in the context of a horror revelation is devastating character comedy — he genuinely may not understand why this is bad, or he's already moving on.

jokes.text: "Hey, but, yo, I did get laid last night. That's lit."
jokes.setup: Aidan is recapping his punishment
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he got laid — by Dee, who thought she was seducing Karen's adult husband
jokes.explanation: The convergence moment — the audience realizes Dee slept with Aidan (a minor), not Karen's adult husband. The casual teen delivery of 'That's lit' makes it land harder. This is a perfectly constructed collision of two plotlines. The horror of the implication is very IASIP.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God. You're the creepy old man from Aidan's Instagram stories." / "Aidan and I are study buddies."
jokes.setup: Karen calls the police; Frank appears
jokes.punchline: Karen recognizes Frank from the Instagram — 'creepy old man' — and Frank's innocent-sounding defense ('study buddies') makes it worse
jokes.explanation: 'Study buddies' as Frank's defense for his relationship with a teenage boy, in a context where Karen already knows about the porn Instagram, is excellent. The wholesome framing applied to something manifestly unwholesome is classic IASIP's approach to Frank's obliviousness. 'Creepy old man from Aidan's Instagram' is a good line too.

jokes.text: High schooler: 'Yo, I'm gonna steal my dad's vape pen. I know where he hides that shit.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is fleeing/escalating their bad situations
jokes.punchline: Aidan's contribution to the chaos is stealing his dad's vape pen — the smallest, most mundane act of teenage rebellion in a scene full of adults doing actually terrible things
jokes.explanation: Good juxtaposition. Adults are fleeing a sex scandal involving a minor, and the teenager's grand escalation is stealing a vape pen. The bathos is sharp.

jokes.text: "Your husband's taking driver's ed? Well, I tell you what, I showed him how to drive stick last night."
jokes.setup: Dee has just told Karen's group that Karen's husband (who Dee thinks she slept with) takes driver's ed
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'drive stick' double entendre — both a driving reference and a sexual boast — implies Frank also had sex, adding another layer of horror
jokes.explanation: Sharp wordplay that merges the two plotlines — driver's ed and the sex storyline — in one double entendre. 'Drive stick' is a legitimately clever bit of wordplay and the reveal that Frank apparently ALSO slept with someone from the story is a good escalation. The driving metaphor paying off as a sex pun earns its keep.

jokes.text: Dennis at John's apartment: 'It has been a long-ass day. It is definitely beer o'clock.' — John: 'There is always Coors in the garage fridge, bro.' — Dennis: 'Clutch!'
jokes.setup: Dennis has spent the episode in identity crisis
jokes.punchline: He has completely adopted the economy man lifestyle — 'beer o'clock,' 'Coors in the garage fridge,' saying 'Clutch!' — the full transformation
jokes.explanation: Good character transformation beat. Dennis saying 'Clutch!' with apparent sincerity is a small but perfect marker of his identity drift. The specificity of Coors in the garage fridge as the pinnacle of Dennis's new world is very funny.

jokes.text: "Can I... can I purchase it from... I will purchase it from you. The Blue Book value, I'll give you double."
jokes.setup: John mentions he might donate the Range Rover
jokes.punchline: Dennis's composure cracks immediately and completely — he stutters, he escalates the offer, he reveals the depth of his yearning
jokes.explanation: Dennis's complete personality reversal in the face of the Range Rover is well-played. His entire 'economy' rebranding evaporates instantly. The stutter and the volunteer of 'double Blue Book' reveals how desperate he still is.

jokes.text: Dennis to John: 'I think I'm gonna donate it to the fire department or something.' — then immediately accepts John's offer to buy it for double Blue Book
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he doesn't want the Range Rover anymore (maintaining his economy persona for John)
jokes.punchline: He sells it to John instantly the moment John offers money, exposing his pose as pure performance
jokes.explanation: Good character hypocrisy beat. Dennis's 'economy man' persona evaporates immediately at the transaction. 'The fire department or something' as a fake charity gesture is perfectly offhand.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Be gone from me now.' / 'Be gone from me, you soy boy beta cuck. The transaction is complete. Be gone!'
jokes.setup: John is confused by Dennis's sudden 180 personality shift
jokes.punchline: Dennis drops all pretense and returns to full alpha mode, using the exact internet incel vocabulary while ordering John out of his sight
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Be gone from me, you soy boy beta cuck' is an exceptional character moment — Dennis's true vocabulary exposed. The formal 'The transaction is complete. Be gone!' is hilariously regal. The contrast with his 'economy man' performance makes this a knockout. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie are fleeing from police/parents on a stolen child's bike while 'Never Gonna Give You Up' plays — Dennis pulls up in the Range Rover
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie stole a kid's bike; Dennis reclaimed his Range Rover
jokes.punchline: Dennis arrives blasting Rick Astley as the getaway car — everyone reunites in the Range Rover as if order is restored
jokes.explanation: Great closing visual. The Range Rover as the reunifying symbol — identities restored — with Rick Astley playing is an absurdist choice that works. The escalating chaos (Mac thinks he killed a kid) being waved away by 'You're in the Range Rover now. All is well' is a perfect dark button.

jokes.text: Mac: 'We did a bad thing, dude. I think I killed a kid.' Charlie: 'He did. I saw him. I think the kid's dead.' Dennis: 'Doesn't matter. Doesn't matter.'
jokes.setup: Everyone piles into the Range Rover while fleeing various crimes
jokes.punchline: Mac's casual admission of possible vehicular manslaughter is treated as a minor detail; Dennis's 'Doesn't matter' is the perfect dark dismissal
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest and best jokes in the episode. The casualness of 'I think I killed a kid' as a throwaway confession, backed by Charlie's earnest eyewitness corroboration, and Dennis's perfect 'Doesn't matter' — this is precisely the show's dark humor working at its best. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: "We almost got T-boned by an Asian. It was totally my fault. She did everything by the book. Very surprising."
jokes.setup: Frank has just had a driving incident
jokes.punchline: Frank admits it was completely his fault — directly contradicting his earlier driver's ed speech about Asians — the driver 'did everything by the book'
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the driver's ed joke. Frank's racist 'wisdom' is proven wrong in exactly the scenario he described, and he admits it with casual matter-of-factness: 'totally my fault, she did everything by the book, very surprising.' The 'very surprising' — as if he's updating his data rather than recognizing his prejudice was simply wrong — is a great character note. Frank can't even process this as a lesson; it's just a surprising data point. Structurally very strong callback.

jokes.text: "Also, Dee banged a kid." / "Ah." / "No, no, I was trying to cuck a bitch..." / "It doesn't matter. It's okay. You're in the Range Rover now. All is well."
jokes.setup: Everyone is in the Range Rover sharing the disaster recaps
jokes.punchline: Dee banging a minor is casually mentioned, Dee protests her framing, and Dennis dismisses the entire catastrophe — including apparent statutory issues — because they're in the Range Rover
jokes.explanation: 'You're in the Range Rover now. All is well.' is an extraordinary punchline. Dennis declaring that the car retroactively resolves all disasters — including apparent crimes — is the perfect thematic conclusion to his entire arc. The vehicle-as-identity theme becomes the vehicle-as-absolution. It's funny, dark, and character-perfect. High quotability. One of the best lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Dee explains to Frank what she was doing: 'I was trying to cuck a bitch.' Dennis: 'It doesn't matter. It's okay. You're in the Range Rover now. All is well.'
jokes.setup: Dee needs to explain her Aidan situation
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts off all moral reckoning with 'You're in the Range Rover now. All is well' — the car as absolute moral absolution
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and a perfect thematic button. 'You're in the Range Rover now. All is well' crystallizes the entire episode's thesis about cars-as-identity into a single absurd statement. It also works as dark comedy because actual crimes have just been committed and this is the resolution. Highly quotable. Strong claim to the episode's best line.

jokes.text: Also in the Range Rover escape — 'We almost got T-boned by an Asian. It was totally my fault. She did everything by the book. Very surprising.'
jokes.setup: Frank spent the episode in driver's ed ranting about Asian drivers
jokes.punchline: Frank's near-accident was entirely his fault and the Asian driver 'did everything by the book' — a perfect ironic callback to his racist theory
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. Frank's driving racism is immediately refuted by his own driving experience — he was at fault, she did everything right. 'Very surprising' is a perfect button showing he still doesn't learn. Great structure and economy.

tmdb_overview: Dee gets in with a group of cool, rich housewives. Dennis hits it off with some everyday blue-collar bros. Frank struggles to renew his license, and Charlie and Mac deal with a new generation of bicycle bullies.
